abstract: Humans learn many context-dependent behaviors; yet the contexts driving these behavior are rarely explicit and must instead be inferred. Further, we are rarely exposed to the same context multiple times, so we must learn how to generalize to new contexts from our experiences in prior ones. Motor learning relies on both. People can hold multiple conflicting visuomotor mappings and recall the appropriate mapping when needed. Much as cricket is easier to learn for someone who already plays baseball, experience with previous mappings accelerates learning of others. Indeed, human motor learning is well described by context inference, in which the learner infers the context and uses it to update and recall the appropriate memory. How the brain implements this inference, and which circuits perform it, however, is unknown. Here we introduce a circuit in which a cerebellar forward model predicts the next state conditioned on a latent from the medial temporal lobe. At the same time, the medial temporal lobe updates that latent from the cerebellum's prediction error. While we only trained the circuit to predict next state, it learns to infer context and represents contexts in a structured latent space. Coupled with this latent, a motor cortex module reproduces context-dependent retrieval, savings after washout, spontaneous recovery, and evoked recovery, and compensates for perturbations it has never experienced. The same circuit reproduces cerebellar-dependence of object-location memory and independence in object-recognition memory, loss of place-cell stability in the dark when cerebellar plasticity is blocked, and the abstract geometry of hippocampal activity in a reversal task. Cerebellar-medial temporal lobe interaction is therefore a candidate locus for context inference and structure learning in the brain.
